input:
In this worked example, we will delve into the calculation of the half-life of a first-order reaction, together with the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by means of the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, where ln(2) is a constant of the relation, and the fraction remaining after a time t (min) is given by exp(-k t). The measured rate constant in this case is k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min.

Substituting the measured value into the half-life relation, we obtain t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.069, which gives t1/2 = 10 min. Turning now to the fraction remaining, the exponential relation can be evaluated at t = 60 min, and the result is a fraction remaining of 0.02 (dimensionless), meaning that only a very small proportion of the original reactant is still present at that point. In other words, the fraction remaining after the stated interval is 0.02, and the half-life from which the decay is counted is 10 min. It is interesting to note that the half-life provides a useful cross-check on this result, since after each successive half-life the remaining fraction is halved once again.

It is important to emphasise, however, that these relations hold only for a first-order reaction; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and the values obtained here cannot simply be transferred to such a case. Overall, the example demonstrates how a single measured rate constant can be utilised to characterise the entire decay behaviour of a first-order system in a straightforward and effective manner.

Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction from a measured rate constant, and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The half-life is 10 min and the fraction remaining at that time is 0.02; both results are obtained from the rate constant in the steps below.

The rate constant is k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, k fixes the half-life t1/2 by the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k: the half-life is the time at which the concentration reaches one half of its initial value, and ln(2) is the constant that the relation carries. Substitution of the measured rate constant gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.069 = 10 min.

The fraction remaining after time t is exp(-k t), with the same rate constant. At t = 60 min, exp(-k t) evaluates to 0.02, dimensionless. The check is internal: at t = t1/2 the fraction remaining must read one half, and the exponential relation returns that value there, so the two relations are consistent at the point where they overlap. The halving reading and the exponential reading are two statements of the same decay, and they agree at every time at which both are evaluated.

Both relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither result transfers to it.
